rules.question: Does `added_code` create a new object inline for an `@ObservedObject` property (e.g. `@ObservedObject var model = ProfileModel()`), so the view owns an object SwiftUI may recreate on every re-render, instead of using `@StateObject` (or `@State` with an `@Observable` class)?
rules.true: An `@ObservedObject` property is initialized with a new instance inside the view.
rules.false: Owned objects use `@StateObject` or `@State`, and `@ObservedObject` is only used for objects passed in from outside.
rules.fix: Use `@StateObject` (or `@State` for `@Observable`) for objects the view creates.

rules.question: Does `added_code` declare a SwiftUI `@State` or `@StateObject` property that is not `private` and is meant to be set by the parent view (for example `@State var user: User` with no default value, filled in through the initializer)?
rules.true: View-owned state is exposed and initialized from outside, so later parent updates are silently ignored.
rules.false: All `@State`/`@StateObject` properties are `private` with local defaults, and data from the parent comes in as `let`, `@Binding`, or an environment value.
rules.fix: Make @State private; take parent data as `let` or `@Binding`.

rules.question: Does `added_code` do expensive work inside a SwiftUI view's `body` (or a computed property or helper that `body` calls each render) — creating a `DateFormatter`, `NumberFormatter`, `JSONDecoder`, or regex; sorting or filtering a large collection; decoding data; or reading files?
rules.true: Work that should be cached or done once runs on every render of the view.
rules.false: Formatters and decoders are static or cached, heavy work happens in the model or a `.task`, or the body only lays out views.
rules.fix: Cache formatters as static properties and move heavy work into the model or `.task`.

rules.question: Does `added_code` start async work with `Task { ... }` inside a SwiftUI `.onAppear` modifier instead of using the `.task` modifier, which cancels automatically when the view disappears?
rules.true: `.onAppear { Task { await ... } }` launches work that is never cancelled.
rules.false: Async work starts in `.task` / `.task(id:)`, or the Task is stored and cancelled in `.onDisappear`, or there is no async work in onAppear.
rules.fix: Use `.task { await ... }` so the work is cancelled with the view.

rules.question: Does `added_code` store or register an escaping closure that captures `self` strongly inside a class — a `Timer` block, a `NotificationCenter` observer block, a Combine `sink` stored in `cancellables`, or a closure assigned to a property — without `[weak self]` or `[unowned self]`, creating a retain cycle?
rules.true: A long-lived closure owned (directly or indirectly) by self references self strongly.
rules.false: Such closures capture `[weak self]`/`[unowned self]`, or the closures are non-escaping or one-shot (map, forEach, withAnimation, a single URLSession or DispatchQueue call), or the code is a SwiftUI struct.
rules.fix: Capture `[weak self]` in stored or registered closures and cancel them when done.

rules.question: Does `added_code` do blocking work on the main thread or in UI code — `Data(contentsOf:)` or `String(contentsOf:)` on a network URL, `Thread.sleep`, `DispatchSemaphore.wait()`, or a synchronous network request — inside a view, view controller, or `@MainActor` type?
rules.true: UI code blocks the main thread waiting on I/O, a sleep, or a semaphore.
rules.false: Blocking I/O happens off the main actor, or the code uses async APIs such as `URLSession.data(from:)` and `Task.sleep`.
rules.fix: Use async APIs (URLSession.data, Task.sleep) or move the work off the main actor.

rules.question: Does `added_code` use `withCheckedContinuation`, `withCheckedThrowingContinuation`, or an unsafe continuation in a way where some path could resume the continuation more than once, or never resume it (for example a callback that can fire repeatedly, or an early `return` / error branch that skips `resume`)?
rules.true: At least one code path resumes twice or not at all.
rules.false: Every path resumes exactly once, or no continuations are used. A continuation stored in a property that another call could overwrite, or a bridge without a cancellation handler, are separate rules and do not count here: answer yes only if a path in the added code itself calls resume twice or returns without resuming.
rules.fix: Make sure every path resumes exactly once; guard repeated callbacks and resume on errors.

rules.question: Does `added_code` declare mutable state that is shared across threads or tasks — a `static var`, a global `var`, or a mutable property on a class singleton or cache used from background queues or concurrent tasks — without an actor, a lock, a serial queue, or `@MainActor` protecting it?
rules.true: Shared mutable state can be read and written concurrently with no synchronization.
rules.false: Shared state is inside an actor, guarded by a lock/serial queue/Mutex, main-actor isolated, or immutable (`let`).
rules.fix: Put the state in an actor, guard it with a lock, or isolate it to the main actor.

rules.question: Does `added_code` use SwiftUI `ForEach` with `id: \.self` over values that may not be unique or that change (model structs, user-editable strings, duplicate values), or over `indices` of a collection that can be modified, instead of a stable identifier?
rules.true: ForEach identifies rows by value or index for data that can change or repeat.
rules.false: Rows use an `Identifiable` stable id, or `id: \.self` is used on a fixed set of unique constants (enum cases, a static range).
rules.fix: Make the model Identifiable with a stable id and use it in ForEach.

rules.question: Does `added_code` call `DispatchQueue.main.async` (or `DispatchQueue.global().async`) from inside an `async` function or a `Task`, mixing Grand Central Dispatch into Swift concurrency code instead of using `await MainActor.run` or `@MainActor`?
rules.true: Async/await code hops threads with DispatchQueue instead of actors.
rules.false: Async code uses `MainActor.run`, `@MainActor`, or actors; DispatchQueue appears only in callback-based (non-async) code, or not at all.
rules.fix: Use `await MainActor.run { }` or mark the type/function `@MainActor`.

rules.question: Does `added_code` wrap a callback- or delegate-based operation (an upload, download, request, location or permission call) in `withCheckedContinuation` / `withCheckedThrowingContinuation` without `withTaskCancellationHandler` or any other way to cancel the underlying operation, so cancelling the Swift task leaves that work running and the caller waiting?
rules.true: A continuation bridges long-running callback work but cancelling the task does not cancel the work.
rules.false: The bridge uses `withTaskCancellationHandler` (or registers a cancel hook) to stop the underlying operation, or the wrapped call is instant and cannot be cancelled, or no continuation is used.
rules.fix: Wrap the bridge in withTaskCancellationHandler and cancel the underlying operation in onCancel.

rules.question: Does `added_code` store a continuation in an instance property (for example `self.continuation = continuation`) where a second concurrent call can overwrite the first stored continuation before it is resumed, leaving the first caller suspended forever?
rules.true: A single stored continuation property can be replaced by a concurrent call, stranding the earlier caller.
rules.false: Concurrent calls are rejected or queued while one is pending, continuations are kept per request (for example in a dictionary keyed by id), or the continuation is only a local variable.
rules.fix: Reject or queue calls while a continuation is pending, or key continuations by request id.

rules.question: Does `added_code` add a test (an `XCTestCase` method named `test…` or a Swift Testing `@Test` function) that could not fail if the code it is named after were broken, because it (a) has no `XCTAssert…`/`#expect`/`#require` at all, (b) only asserts a tautology or a value the test itself just created (`XCTAssertTrue(true)`, `XCTAssertNotNil(Foo())`, `#expect(x == x)`), (c) only checks that a mock or stub returns what the test configured it to return, or that a method the test called directly was called, or (d) replaces the very type or function it claims to test with a fake?
rules.true: At least one added test has no assertion that depends on the real behaviour of the code under test: no assertion, a tautology, an assertion on the test's own stub or input, or the unit under test is itself faked.
rules.false: Every added test calls real code and asserts on its output, thrown error, published state, or a side effect it causes (including calls the unit under test makes to a fake, with arguments the unit computed). Weak but real assertions (`XCTAssertNotNil` on a computed result) do not count. Test helpers, fakes, fixtures and setUp code without test methods do not count, and neither does code that is not a test.
rules.fix: Make the test exercise the real code and assert on a result that would change if that code broke; delete it if it can't.
